courseMetadata.title: Observability & Debugging in Production
courseMetadata.description: A hands-on course for senior developers. Instrument a real-shaped app (**Brewline**, a coffee pre-order service) with structured logs, request correlation, RED metrics and end-to-end traces from browser to database. Then debug three seeded production bugs, an intermittent 500, a slow endpoint and a broken frontend state, using *only* the telemetry you built: no debugger, no local repro, no guessing from the code. Runnable JavaScript and SQL throughout.

prerequisites.description: Comfortable building and deploying an HTTP backend (the examples use **Node.js**) and a browser frontend that calls it with `fetch`.
Reads and writes modern JavaScript, including `async`/`await` and Promises.
Has written unit tests with `describe`/`it`/`expect` or a similar framework.

interleavingGroups.rationaleNote: Logging and correlation items resurface during the log-driven investigation, so learners retrieve the schema and correlation rules exactly when they need them.
Percentiles, self-time and N+1 reasoning are interleaved so learners discriminate 'what the dashboard says' from 'where the trace says the time went'.
Propagation and client telemetry are retrieved inside the frontend-state investigation.
Cardinality, PII, sampling and gap-closing recur at rising Bloom levels, from hygiene to design to reflection.

competencies.title: Emit structured, queryable logs
competencies.description: Replace free-text logging with machine-parseable events: consistent field names, severity levels, event-oriented messages, and logging at meaningful boundaries rather than everywhere.

desiredOutcomes.description: Refactor free-text logs into schema-conforming events with correct levels, fixed event names and redacted fields.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Scores 80%+ on the structured-logging assessment and meets the success criteria of the hospital-lab transfer exercise.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: More logging is always safer.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Volume without structure buries the signal, raises ingest and storage cost and slows every query. Useful logs are chosen at boundaries (request in/out, external calls) and decisions (a retry, a fallback), not on every line.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Redo the worked example 'Refactoring checkout logs into events' (refactoring four checkout log lines into one event per outcome) and name the production question each surviving event answers.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Structured logging just means JSON output.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: JSON is only a format. The value comes from a stable schema: fixed, low-variety event names, consistent keys and types, and variable data in separate fields. `{"msg": "Order 8812 failed"}` is JSON and still unqueryable.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Re-run the error-serialisation prediction (Section 1) (an Error serialises to `{}`) and complete the `toLogEvent` challenge, which enforces the schema.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Log levels are cosmetic.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Levels drive sampling, retention and alerting. Logging expected outcomes (a declined card, a 404) as `error` fires alerts for things nobody must fix, so on-call learns to ignore errors and misses the real ones.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Review the Brewline level table and classify five sample events (declined card, DB write failed, fallback price used, order created, pricing rule trace).

competencies.title: Correlate telemetry to a single request
competencies.description: Generate, propagate and attach a request/correlation ID to every log line and outbound call, and make context survive async boundaries.

desiredOutcomes.description: Implement request-ID generation and propagation so every log line and outbound call for one request carries the same ID, including across `await`.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Passes the correlation assessment and the child-logger test-suite challenge.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Timestamps are enough to line up what happened.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Concurrent requests interleave in time, and clocks on different instances (and in browsers) drift. Timestamps tell you *when*, not *whose*; only a shared ID reliably groups events.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Revisit the worked example 'Proving correlation survives concurrency': B's lines finish before A's, yet filtering by `requestId` returns each request's lines exactly.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Setting the ID once at the entry point is enough.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: An ID stored in shared state is overwritten by the next request while the first is paused at `await`, and it stops at your service's edge unless it is sent onward in a header. Context must be per request and explicitly propagated.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Re-run the shared-request-ID prediction (Section 1) (module-level ID) and fix the `createLogger` child-isolation bug in the logger 'make the failing tests pass' challenge.

competencies.title: Instrument code with counters, gauges and histograms
competencies.description: Choose the right metric type, name metrics and labels well, and record latency and error rates at service boundaries.

desiredOutcomes.description: Add a request counter, an error counter and a latency histogram at the HTTP boundary using only bounded-cardinality labels.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Passes the metrics assessment and the `normalizeRoute`/`redSummary` challenges.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Averages describe latency well.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: An average blends fast and slow requests into a number that describes nobody. Nine 50 ms requests and one 2.4 s request average 286 ms; p50 (51 ms) and p99 (2,400 ms) show what users actually experience.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Re-run the average-vs-percentile predict exercise and compute p50/p99 with `redSummary`.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Labels are free, so put user IDs or URLs with IDs in them.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Every distinct label value creates a new time series. A `userId` label on a 180-series histogram with 200,000 users makes 36 million series, enough to slow down or crash a metrics backend and multiply the bill.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Redo the 'Choosing labels that won't explode' worked example's cardinality arithmetic and complete the `normalizeRoute` challenge.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Metrics and logs are interchangeable.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Metrics are cheap aggregates that tell you *that* something is wrong; logs and traces carry per-event detail that tells you *why*. Per-user or per-order questions belong in logs and traces.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Sort ten production questions into 'metric' or 'log/trace' and explain each choice.

competencies.title: Build and read a service-health dashboard
competencies.description: Assemble a minimal RED dashboard that separates normal from abnormal behaviour, and read percentile and rate charts correctly against a baseline.

desiredOutcomes.description: Build a RED dashboard and state from it whether the service is healthy, citing specific percentile and error-rate values against a baseline.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Passes the dashboards assessment, including the written health statement.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A dashboard should show every metric we have.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: A dashboard exists to answer a few questions fast (is it healthy, where, errors or slowness?). Forty panels hide the one that moved.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Rebuild the four-panel RED dashboard and delete any panel that does not answer one of its three questions.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Percentiles can be averaged across instances or time windows.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Percentiles are not additive. The average of a 200 ms p99 and a 1,800 ms p99 is not the fleet p99; it must be computed from merged histogram buckets.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Work the two-instance p99 problem again, merging bucket counts before computing the percentile.

competencies.title: Trace a request across service boundaries
competencies.description: Create spans with meaningful names and attributes, propagate W3C trace context from browser to backend to database, and interpret the resulting waterfall.

desiredOutcomes.description: Produce one connected trace per user action from browser to database, and attribute latency to a specific span using self-time.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Passes the tracing assessment and one tracing transfer exercise.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Tracing is only for microservices.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Even a single API has boundaries where time and errors hide: browser → network → API → database → payment provider. The number of boundaries, not services, makes tracing valuable.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Draw Brewline's Place Order trace and label each boundary where the 8-second delay could hide.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Auto-instrumentation gives you everything.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Auto-instrumentation records generic HTTP and SQL spans. It cannot see business steps (pricing, inventory reservation) or attach business attributes (`store.id`), so unexplained self-time is exactly where your own code hides.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Redo the worked example 'Filling the gap in an auto-instrumented trace': find the 790 ms of unexplained self-time and place manual spans.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Span duration equals work done in that service.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: A span's duration includes time waiting on its children, and parallel children overlap. Attribute latency by self-time (duration minus the union of child intervals).
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Re-run the parallel-children predict exercise (−75 ms) and complete the `selfTime` challenge.

competencies.title: Make client-side behaviour observable
competencies.description: Capture frontend errors, key user actions and state transitions as telemetry linked to the backend trace, so 'the UI is broken' can be investigated without the user's machine.

desiredOutcomes.description: Emit client state and error events linked by trace ID and use them to diagnose a UI bug the server never sees.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Passes the frontend assessment and the exam-platform transfer exercise.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If the API returned 200, the frontend is fine.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Broken UI state often comes from valid responses: an older response applied after a newer one, or a field with an unexpected type. None of these produce a server error.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Re-run the 'last response wins' predict exercise and reconstruct session s-31's timeline.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Frontend errors show up in the browser console, so we'll see them.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The console that shows the error is the customer's, and you will never see it. Client errors and state transitions must be captured deliberately and shipped (e.g., with `sendBeacon`) with the active trace ID.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: List the four client signals Brewline captures and how each is shipped and linked.

competencies.title: Query logs, metrics and traces to answer specific questions
competencies.description: Filter, aggregate, group and join telemetry to isolate a subset of requests, compare failing and succeeding cohorts, and pivot between signals.

desiredOutcomes.description: Write cohort queries that compare failing and succeeding requests, and pivot from a metric spike to traces and logs.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Passes the querying assessment and the provider-cohort SQL challenge.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Search for the error message and read the matches.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Reading matches shows symptoms one at a time. Diagnosis comes from comparison: group requests by candidate attributes and ask what failing requests share that succeeding ones do not.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Redo the worked example 'Grouping to find the difference': move from 'the new version' to 'Adyen timeouts' in two cohort queries.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If the query returned nothing, the event didn't happen.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Empty or small results can mean a wrong filter (`status = 500` when failures are 502s), NULLs excluded by `<>`, `AVG`/`COUNT(column)` skipping NULLs, sampling, or an instrumentation gap. Check coverage before concluding absence.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Re-run the NULL predict exercises (P2.2 and P3.1) and compare `COUNT(*)` with `COUNT(column)` on your own data.

competencies.title: Diagnose production bugs from telemetry alone
competencies.description: Run a hypothesis-driven investigation (observe → hypothesize → query → confirm/refute), reach root cause without a debugger or local repro, and document the evidence chain.

desiredOutcomes.description: Diagnose an intermittent 500, a slow endpoint and a broken frontend state using only telemetry, proving root cause with the 'explains all' test.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Passes the diagnosis assessment and the pharmacy-robot transfer exercise; capstone evidence logs meet the rubric.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: I'll find it faster by reading the code.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Code shows what *could* happen; telemetry shows what *did* happen, to whom and under which conditions. Timing-, data- and load-dependent bugs are invisible in code.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Replay Worked Investigation 1 and note which step would have been impossible from the code alone (the harbor × pumpkin-latte interaction).

commonMisconceptions.misconception: The first anomaly I see is the cause.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Correlated symptoms (one instance erroring more, CPU up) are often effects or coincidence. A root cause must explain every failure and no successes.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Score the three hypotheses from Investigation 1 with `scoreHypothesis` and explain why `api-2` fails the test.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Intermittent means random.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Intermittent failures almost always depend on a hidden variable (input data, store, timing, dependency state). Cohort analysis, including combinations of attributes, exposes it.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Re-run the store, item and store × item cohort queries and watch 50% and 57% become 100% and 0%.

competencies.title: Evaluate telemetry cost, safety and coverage trade-offs
competencies.description: Judge sampling strategies, retention, cardinality, PII and secret exposure, and overhead; identify and close the instrumentation gaps an investigation reveals.

desiredOutcomes.description: Choose and justify a sampling policy, keep secrets and unbounded labels out of telemetry, and close investigation gaps with bounded, safe additions.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Passes the trade-offs assessment and the redaction and tail-sampling challenges.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Sample 1% of traces uniformly and you'll be fine.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Uniform head sampling decides before the outcome is known, so it keeps rare errors only at the base rate: 1% of 4,000 daily errors is 40. Tail sampling keeps all errors and slow traces for a similar order of cost.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Redo the 'Choosing a sampling strategy' worked example's arithmetic and implement `shouldKeepTrace`.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: It's internal telemetry, so logging full request bodies is fine.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Telemetry is copied to vendors, retained for months and read by many people, which puts it in PII and PCI scope. Bodies and headers carry emails, card numbers and tokens.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Review the Lab 1 flawed diff and implement `redact` for nested fields.

sectionSummary.content:
## Section 1 summary: what you should now believe

1. A log is useful when it is an **event with a schema**: a fixed event name, typed fields and the right level, emitted at boundaries and decisions.
2. **Correlation is per request and must be propagated**: through async context, into every event, and onward in outbound headers.
3. **Metrics say *that*, logs say *why*.** Counters and histograms with small, fixed label sets give you rate, errors and duration cheaply.
4. **Read tails, not averages**, and compare every number with a baseline. Percentiles come from merged histograms, never from averaging percentiles.
5. **Telemetry has a cost and a blast radius.** Redact secrets and personal data, and keep IDs out of metric labels.
keyTakeaways: Logs are **events with a schema**: fixed names, typed fields, the right level.
Correlation is **per request** and must be **propagated** through async code and outbound headers.
Metrics say *that*; logs and traces say *why*.
Read **p50/p99 against a baseline**, never averages or averaged percentiles.
Keep secrets, personal data and unbounded values **out** of telemetry.

contentBlocks.content:
## Why this matters

It is 2:10 a.m. The Brewline on-call phone buzzes: *"Customers say checkout sometimes fails."* You open the logs and find 40,000 lines like this:

```text
Error processing order
Order failed!!
something went wrong: undefined
```

None of them say which order, which store, which user, how long the request took, or whether the failures share anything. You cannot count them, group them or follow one customer's request from start to finish. So you read the code, guess, add more `console.log` lines, redeploy and wait. That costs hours, sometimes days.

This section fixes the raw material. By the end, every request Brewline handles will produce:

- a small set of **events you can query** ("all failed orders at `harbor` in the last hour, grouped by item")
- a **request ID** that ties together every line that request wrote
- **numbers** that tell you in seconds whether the service is healthy right now

The capstone in Section 3 can only be solved with telemetry, and the telemetry you add here is what you will have to work with.

## What you will be able to do

| # | Objective |
|---|---|
| 1.1 | Refactor free-text log statements into structured events that conform to a defined field schema (event name, level, request ID, duration, outcome). |
| 1.2 | Implement request-ID generation and propagation so every log line for one request, including async work and outbound calls, carries the same ID. |
| 1.3 | Add a request counter, an error counter and a latency histogram at the HTTP boundary, using only bounded-cardinality labels. |
| 1.4 | Build a RED dashboard and explain from it whether the service is currently healthy, citing specific percentile and error-rate values. |
| 1.5 | Identify and remove sensitive fields and high-cardinality labels from a provided flawed instrumentation diff. |

**The example domain.** Every example uses **Brewline**, a coffee pre-order app: a browser frontend, the `brewline-api` Node.js backend (two instances, `api-1` and `api-2`), a database, and the payment providers `stripe` and `adyen`. Stores are `harbor`, `midtown` and `airport`.

**How the code works here.** Examples marked *Run* execute in your browser. Graded challenges check your code automatically; you can re-run as often as you like. The test runner in this course is Jest-compatible, not Jest itself: you can use `describe`, `it`, `expect` with the common matchers, `beforeEach`/`afterEach` and `jest.fn`, but not module mocking, snapshots or fake timers.

### Key terms

- **Log event:** one record describing one thing that happened, stored as named fields rather than a sentence.
- **Field:** a named value on an event, such as `orderId: 8812`.
- **Schema:** the agreed list of field names, their types and meanings, shared by every event in a service (ideally across services).
- **Severity level:** how urgent the event is (`debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error`). Tooling uses it to decide what to keep, what to alert on and what to drop.
- **Structured logging:** emitting log events that follow a schema, so machines can filter, group and count them.

**The Brewline log schema.** Every event from `brewline-api` must have the base fields below. Domain fields are added when relevant.

| Field | Type | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ts` | ISO-8601 string | When the event happened (UTC) | `"2026-09-21T10:15:02.114Z"` |
| `level` | `debug`/`info`/`warn`/`error` | Severity | `"warn"` |
| `event` | string, `noun.verb_past` | What happened; a fixed, low-variety name | `"order.payment_declined"` |
| `service` | string | Which service emitted it | `"brewline-api"` |
| `requestId` | string | Correlation ID for the request (see the correlation lesson) | `"req-7f3a"` |
| `route` | string, templated | Route template, never the raw URL | `"POST /api/orders"` |
| `durationMs` | number | Duration of the operation this event closes | `312` |
| `outcome` | `ok`/`declined`/`error`/… | Result of the operation | `"declined"` |
| domain fields | typed | e.g. `orderId`, `storeId`, `item`, `reason` | `"storeId": "harbor"` |

Notice what is *not* in the `event` field: variable data. `"order.payment_declined"` has the same value for every declined payment, so you can count them. The variable parts (`orderId`, `reason`) go in their own fields.

**Where to log.** Log at **boundaries** (a request arrives or finishes, a call to the database or payment provider returns) and at **decisions** (a branch that changes the outcome, such as a retry or a fallback price). Do not log every line of a loop. More lines do not mean more insight; they mean more cost and more noise to search through.

**What levels mean at Brewline**

| Level | Use it when… | Brewline example | Consequence |
|---|---|---|---|
| `error` | Brewline failed to do its job and someone may need to act | Order could not be saved | Counts toward error alerts |
| `warn` | Something unusual happened but was handled | Payment declined by the customer's bank; fallback price used | Watched, not paged |
| `info` | Normal, meaningful business event | Order created | Kept for investigation |
| `debug` | Detail only useful while developing | Pricing rule evaluation steps | Usually dropped in production |

A declined card is the customer's problem, not Brewline's, so it is `warn`, not `error`. If you log it as `error`, your error alerts fire every time a customer's card is declined. The team learns to ignore them, and then misses the real failure.

contentBlocks.caption: **Run it.** A structured event from the refactored checkout handler. Expected output: one JSON line with `event`, `outcome` and `reason` as separate fields.

interactionSequence.prompt: **Predict before you run.** This event is serialised with `JSON.stringify`. Write down exactly what you expect to be printed, then run it.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
**Actual output:** `{"event":"order.failed","orderId":8812,"err":{}}`

Most people expect to see `"couponCode":undefined` and the error's message. `JSON.stringify` silently **drops keys whose value is `undefined`**. It also serialises only an object's *own enumerable* properties, and an `Error`'s `message` and `stack` are not enumerable, so the error becomes `{}`. The most important field in the event, *why it failed*, vanishes without a warning. JSON output alone does not make logs useful (`structured-logging-m2`). A structured logger must convert errors explicitly to `{ name, message }`, which is what the next challenge asks you to do.

contentBlocks.content:
### Correlation: tying lines to one request

**Concrete problem.** Two customers place orders 3 ms apart. Brewline logs:

```text
10:15:02.101 order.received orderId=8812
10:15:02.104 order.received orderId=8813
10:15:02.139 payment.charged
10:15:02.141 order.failed err="price is null"
```

Which order failed? The `order.failed` line doesn't say. The timestamps don't help either: both requests were in flight at the same moment, and on two instances (`api-1`, `api-2`) the clocks can differ by several milliseconds. Timestamps tell you *when*, not *whose*.

### Key terms

- **Request ID (correlation ID):** a unique value generated once per incoming request and attached to every event that request produces.
- **Propagation:** carrying that ID from one piece of code to the next, including across `await`, callbacks, queues and outbound HTTP calls.
- **Request context:** the per-request data (request ID, user, route) that code deep in the call stack needs without having it passed as an argument everywhere.

**How to do it in Brewline**

1. **Generate or accept.** At the HTTP entry point, read an incoming `x-request-id` header if a trusted upstream (load balancer, frontend) sent one; otherwise generate one.
2. **Store it in request context.** Either create a *child logger* bound to the ID and pass it down, or use Node's `AsyncLocalStorage` so any code in that request's async chain can read it.
3. **Attach it to every event.** The logger adds `requestId` automatically, so developers can't forget it.
4. **Send it onward.** Every outbound HTTP call (payments, inventory) sends `x-request-id` so the next service logs the same ID.
5. **Return it.** Send it back in the response header so support staff can ask a customer for it.

Setting the ID "once at the top" is not enough on its own. You will see exactly how in the prediction exercise below.

## An analogy: luggage tags

A request ID works like the tag an airline puts on your suitcase at check-in. Your bag passes through belts, scanners, carts and a second airport, and every station records the tag number, not "a blue suitcase that arrived around 10:15". Because the tag travels *with* the bag, any station can look up the bag's whole journey. Two things break this: a tag printed once on a shared whiteboard (any bag can be matched to the wrong entry), and a tag that is removed when the bag changes airline (the trail ends at the edge). Those are exactly the two correlation failures in this lesson: shared state, and not propagating the ID onward.

### Metrics: counting instead of reading

Logs describe individual events. Metrics are **numbers aggregated over time**. They are cheap to store and fast to chart, and they tell you *that* something is wrong. Logs (and, in Section 2, traces) tell you *why*. You need both, because they answer different questions.

### Key terms

- **Counter:** a number that only goes up, such as total requests. You chart its *rate* (per second).
- **Gauge:** a number that goes up and down, such as open DB connections or queue length.
- **Histogram:** counts of observations in value ranges called **buckets** (e.g., ≤50 ms, ≤100 ms, ≤250 ms…). Percentiles are computed from it.
- **Percentile (pNN):** the value that NN% of observations are at or below. p99 = 250 ms means 99% of requests took 250 ms or less.
- **Label:** a key–value pair that splits a metric into separate series, such as `route="POST /api/orders"`.
- **Cardinality:** the number of distinct series a metric produces, which is the product of the number of distinct values of each label.
- **RED method:** for every request-serving service, track **R**ate (requests/sec), **E**rrors (failed requests/sec or %) and **D**uration (latency distribution).

**Brewline's three HTTP metrics**

| Metric | Type | Labels |
|---|---|---|
| `http_requests_total` | counter | `route` (templated), `method`, `status_class` (`2xx`,`4xx`,`5xx`) |
| `http_request_errors_total` | counter | `route`, `method` (counts 5xx only) |
| `http_request_duration_ms` | histogram | `route`, `method`; buckets 25, 50, 100, 250, 500, 1000, 2500, 5000 |

### The RED dashboard: reading health at a glance

A dashboard exists to answer a few questions fast: *Is Brewline healthy? If not, which route, and is it errors or slowness?* Brewline's first dashboard has four panels, and nothing else:

1. **Rate** — requests/sec by route.
2. **Error %** — 5xx ÷ all requests, by route.
3. **Latency** — p50 and p99 by route, from the histogram.
4. **Saturation hint** — DB connection-pool usage (a gauge).

Two reading rules:

- **Compare against a baseline**, such as the same hour yesterday or last week. A number on its own tells you nothing.
- **Never average percentiles.** If `api-1` has p99 = 200 ms and `api-2` has p99 = 1,800 ms, the fleet p99 is *not* 1,000 ms. Percentiles must be computed from the **merged histogram** buckets. Most tools do this if you aggregate the histogram, not the percentile series.

workedExamples.problem: A teammate proposes adding `userId` and the raw `path` as labels on `http_request_duration_ms` "so we can debug per user". Evaluate the proposal.
steps: **Count the series for the current labels.** 6 route templates × 3 methods × 1 histogram with 8 buckets (+ sum, count) = 6 × 3 × 10 = **180 series**. Trivial.
**Add `userId`.** Brewline has 200,000 active users: 180 × 200,000 = **36,000,000 series**. Most metric backends slow down or fall over well before that, and the bill grows with series count.
**Add raw `path` instead.** `/api/orders/8812`, `/api/orders/8813`… every order ID becomes a new series. The same explosion, just slower.
**Ask what question the label was meant to answer.** 'Which user had a slow request?' is a *per-event* question, and per-event questions belong in logs and traces, where `userId` is a field.
**Decide.** Keep `route`, `method` and `status_class`. Normalise raw paths to templates (`/api/orders/:id`). Put `userId` in the log event.
workedExamples.conclusion: A label is only safe if its set of possible values is **small and fixed**. IDs, emails, raw URLs and free-text error messages are never labels.

contentBlocks.content:
### Telemetry has costs and risks

Every event and label you add has three costs: **money** (ingest and storage), **performance** (serialising and sending), and **risk** (whatever you log may leak). Telemetry pipelines are copied to vendors, retained for months and read by many people. That makes them a frequent source of leaked emails, card numbers and auth tokens, and they fall within the scope of privacy law and PCI audits.

Brewline's rules:

- Never log request or response **bodies** wholesale.
- Mask known-sensitive keys (`password`, `cardNumber`, `cvv`, `authorization`, `email`) with a redaction step in the logger (you will build it below).
- Log identifiers such as `userId`, not personal data such as `email`.
- Metric labels must come from small fixed sets.

### ⚠️ Common errors

1. **Putting variable data in the event name** (`"order 8812 failed"`). The event can no longer be counted. Keep names fixed and put the data in fields. *(`structured-logging-m2`)*
2. **Logging `error` for expected outcomes** such as declined cards or 404s. Error alerts drown in noise. *(`structured-logging-m3`)*
3. **Logging an `Error` object with `JSON.stringify`.** It serialises to `{}` and the message is lost (see the serialisation prediction exercise). Convert errors to `{ name, message }` explicitly.
4. **Storing the request ID in a module-level variable.** Concurrent requests overwrite it after an `await`. *(`request-correlation-m2`)*
5. **Forgetting outbound calls.** The ID stops at Brewline's edge unless you send `x-request-id` to payments and inventory. *(`request-correlation-m2`)*
6. **Labelling metrics with IDs or raw URLs.** This causes a cardinality explosion. *(`metrics-instrumentation-m2`)*
7. **Charting average latency or averaging p99s across instances.** *(`metrics-instrumentation-m1`, `signal-dashboards-m2`)*
8. **Counting 4xx as server errors.** A 404 for a deleted order is the client's mistake. Error % should count 5xx.
9. **Logging whole request bodies "just for debugging".** *(`instrumentation-tradeoffs-m2`)*

## Misconceptions to watch for in this section

- **"Structured logging just means JSON output"** (`structured-logging-m2`). JSON is a format; the value is a stable schema with fixed event names and typed fields.
- **"Setting the ID once at the entry point is enough"** (`request-correlation-m2`). Shared state is overwritten across `await`, and the ID stops at your edge unless you send it onward.
- **"Labels are free"** (`metrics-instrumentation-m2`). Every distinct label value is a new time series.
- **"Averages describe latency well"** (`metrics-instrumentation-m1`). Averages describe nobody; use p50 and p99.
- **"It's internal telemetry, so logging full request bodies is fine"** (`instrumentation-tradeoffs-m2`). Telemetry is copied, retained and widely read.

## Lab 1: Instrument `brewline-api` (practical activity, about 45 minutes)

**Goal:** every request to `brewline-api` produces schema-conforming events carrying one request ID, and a four-panel RED dashboard shows live health.

**Setup:** run the Brewline reference app and its load generator (a steady mix of menu, cart, order and history requests). Any log viewer and metrics backend will do; logs must be queryable as JSON and metrics scraped from `/metrics`.

1. **Inventory (5 min).** List every `console.log` in the order and history handlers and write the production question each answers, or "none".
2. **Logger (10 min).** Build a logger on your `toLogEvent` and `redact` functions. Emit `order.created`, `order.payment_declined`, `order.failed` and `http.request_completed` with the full base schema. Delete the lines that answered "none".
3. **Correlation (10 min).** Add middleware that accepts or generates `x-request-id`, stores it in request context and returns it in the response header. Send it to the payments client. Verify with 20 concurrent orders: filtering by one `requestId` must show exactly that request's lines.
4. **Metrics (10 min).** Add `http_requests_total`, `http_request_errors_total` and the `http_request_duration_ms` histogram, labelled only by `normalizeRoute(path)`, `method` and `status_class`.
5. **Dashboard (5 min).** Build the four RED panels, with p50 and p99 computed from the histogram.
6. **Review a flawed diff (5 min).** Answer the scenario question below.

**Acceptance checklist**

- One request's complete log lines, filtered by `requestId`, exported or screenshotted.
- Every event has `ts`, `level`, `event`, `service`, `requestId`, `route`, and `durationMs`/`outcome` where it closes an operation.
- No event contains `email`, `cardNumber`, `cvv` or `authorization` values.
- Under 200 series for the three HTTP metrics combined.
- A two-sentence health statement citing an error % and a p99 value.

## Section 1 summary: what you should now believe

1. A log is useful when it is an **event with a schema**: a fixed event name, typed fields and the right level, emitted at boundaries and decisions.
2. **Correlation is per request and must be propagated**: through async context, into every event, and onward in outbound headers.
3. **Metrics say *that*, logs say *why*.** Counters and histograms with small, fixed label sets give you rate, errors and duration cheaply.
4. **Read tails, not averages**, and compare every number with a baseline. Percentiles come from merged histograms, never from averaging percentiles.

## Why this matters

After Section 1, Brewline's API logs are clean and correlated. Then a support ticket arrives: *"I pressed Place Order, the spinner ran for 8 seconds, and then the page said my cart was empty."*

Where did those 8 seconds go? The API log says `http.request_completed durationMs=240`. Was the time spent in the browser, the network, the payment provider or the database? And the "empty cart" never shows up in any server log, because it happened in the customer's browser.

A request ID in API logs covers one hop of a journey that starts with a click and passes through a browser, an API, a database and a payment provider. **Distributed tracing** records the whole journey as one timeline. **Frontend telemetry** puts the browser's side of the story in the same place. With both, "why did *this* click take 8 seconds and end in an empty cart?" can be answered from data. In Section 3 you will need exactly this to debug a broken frontend state that the server never sees.

## What you will be able to do

| # | Objective |
|---|---|
| 2.1 | Add manual spans with business-meaningful names and attributes around key backend operations, complementing auto-instrumentation. |
| 2.2 | Propagate trace context from a browser fetch through the backend to database calls, producing one connected trace per user action. |
| 2.3 | Capture frontend errors and key state transitions as telemetry linked to the originating trace ID. |
| 2.4 | Interpret a trace waterfall to attribute latency to a specific span, distinguishing self-time from time spent waiting on children. |
| 2.5 | Write queries that filter, group and compare telemetry cohorts and pivot from a metric spike to exemplar traces and their logs. |
| 2.6 | Choose and justify a sampling strategy that keeps error and slow traces while bounding volume. |

**Builds on Section 1:** the request ID becomes a trace ID, the structured events become span attributes and linked logs, and the RED dashboard becomes the starting point for pivoting to traces.

### What a trace is, starting from one click

**Concrete picture.** The customer clicks **Place Order**. Here is what Brewline records as a trace:

```text
trace 4bf92f35…  (one user action)
├─ [browser] click "Place Order"                         0 ──────────────────────── 310 ms
│  └─ [browser] fetch POST /api/orders                     8 ─────────────────────── 300
│     └─ [api] POST /api/orders                             20 ──────────────────── 290
│        ├─ [api] pricing.calculate                          22 ── 30
│        ├─ [db]  db.insert orders                           31 ───── 60
│        └─ [api] payments.charge  provider=stripe           62 ─────────────── 280
│           └─ [http] POST https://api.stripe…/charges        64 ────────────── 278
```

### Key terms

- **Trace:** the full record of one operation (usually one user action or one incoming request) as it moves through every component. It is identified by a **trace ID**.
- **Span:** one timed unit of work inside a trace, such as "insert into orders" or "call Stripe". It has a name, start time, duration, a **span ID**, its **parent span ID**, a **status** (ok/error) and **attributes**.
- **Attributes:** key–value details on a span, such as `store.id=harbor`, `order.item_count=3` or `payment.provider=stripe`. They play the same role as structured log fields.
- **Root span:** the span with no parent, where the trace began.
- **Waterfall:** the timeline view above, with each span drawn as a bar under its parent.
Tracing is not only for microservices. Brewline is one API plus a browser and a database, and it already has four boundaries (browser → network → API → DB/payments) where time and errors can hide.

### Auto-instrumentation and manual spans

**Auto-instrumentation** means libraries (e.g., OpenTelemetry's HTTP, Express and database plugins) that create spans automatically for every incoming request, outgoing HTTP call and SQL query. It is the fastest way to get a connected skeleton, so turn it on first.

It cannot know your business logic, though. Auto spans are named `POST /api/orders` or `SELECT`. They don't say *pricing* versus *inventory reservation*, and they don't carry `store.id` or `order.item_count`. When the slow part of a request is your own code, or when the question is "which stores?", the auto trace has a gap exactly where you need detail.

**Manual spans** fill those gaps. Two naming rules, borrowed from Section 1:

- **Span names are low-variety**, like event names: `pricing.calculate`, never `pricing for order 8812`.
- **Variable data goes in attributes**, like log fields: `order.id=8812`, `store.id=harbor`.

contentBlocks.content:
### Context propagation: one trace from browser to database

A trace only connects if every hop passes along **trace context**: the trace ID, the current span ID (which becomes the next hop's parent) and the sampling decision. The standard carrier is the **W3C `traceparent` header**:

```text
traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01
             ^^ ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ ^^
          version        trace ID (16 bytes)     parent span ID   flags (01 = sampled)
```

Section 1's request ID worked the same way: generate at the edge, carry through context, send onward. `traceparent` is the standardised, richer version of `x-request-id`. Many teams set the log's `requestId` equal to the trace ID so logs and traces join directly.

**The four Brewline hops**

1. **Browser → API.** The frontend's tracing library starts a span for the click, and its fetch instrumentation adds `traceparent` to the request. Browsers only send custom headers cross-origin if the API allows them: the API's CORS response must include `traceparent` in `Access-Control-Allow-Headers`, and the tracing library must be told which API URLs to propagate to. If either is missing, the header silently isn't sent and the trace breaks into two.
2. **API entry.** Server middleware reads `traceparent`, validates it (you will write the validator below) and makes the incoming span the parent of the server span. If the header is missing or invalid, it starts a new trace.
3. **Inside the API.** Context flows through async code the same way the request ID did in Section 1 (OpenTelemetry uses AsyncLocalStorage in Node). Every DB query and outbound call becomes a child span.
4. **API → payments / queues.** The outbound HTTP instrumentation injects `traceparent`. For a queue, put it in the message headers so the consumer can continue the trace.

### Frontend observability: the part of the story the server never sees

From Brewline's servers, a request that returned `200 OK` in 90 ms looks perfect. But the customer may still see a broken page:

- the response was valid, but the UI code mishandled a field (e.g., `eta_seconds` arrived as a string)
- two responses arrived out of order and the older one overwrote the newer one
- a JavaScript exception was thrown while rendering

None of this reaches a server log. The exception appears in *the customer's* browser console, which you will never see. Frontend telemetry must be **deliberately captured and shipped**.

**What Brewline captures in the browser**

| Signal | How | Linked by |
|---|---|---|
| Uncaught errors | `window.addEventListener("error", …)` and `"unhandledrejection"` | `sessionId`, active `traceId` |
| Key state transitions | `cart.state_changed` from → to (e.g., `submitting` → `confirmed`) | `sessionId`, `seq`, `traceId` of the request that caused it |
| Requests sent / responses applied | `cart.request_sent`, `cart.response_applied` with `cart_items` | `traceId` of that fetch |
| User actions | `checkout.clicked` | `sessionId`, `seq` |

Two design details matter:

- **Sequence numbers (`seq`).** Browser clocks are unreliable. A per-session counter records the true order of events on that device.
- **Shipping.** Batch events and send them with `navigator.sendBeacon` (or a keep-alive fetch) so they survive the tab closing.

The shared **`traceId`** is what makes this powerful: from a broken client state you can jump straight to the backend trace for the request that caused it, and back again.

Browser clocks are unreliable and can't link to a backend trace.
You will never see customers' consoles.
A 200 says nothing about what the UI did with the response.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Client telemetry is only useful when it is **ordered** (`seq`) and **linked** (`traceId`). Then a broken state leads straight to the request behind it.

contentBlocks.content:
### Reading a waterfall

A span's **duration** is wall-clock time from start to end. It includes time spent waiting on child spans.

- **Self-time:** the part of a span's duration not covered by any child. This is time spent in that span's own code, or in work nobody instrumented.
- **Child time:** time covered by at least one child.

Reading rule: **find the span with the largest self-time**, not the span with the largest duration. The root span always has the largest duration, and that tells you nothing about where the time went.

contentBlocks.caption: **Run it.** Duration versus self-time for a checkout trace with sequential children.

interactionSequence.prompt: **Predict before you run.** The history endpoint runs two DB queries in parallel with `Promise.all`. This code computes the parent's self-time as *duration minus the sum of child durations*. What does it print?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
**Actual output:** `self time = -75 ms`

"Self-time = parent − children" is only right when children run **one after another**. Here the two queries overlap almost entirely, so their sum (175 ms) exceeds the parent's duration (100 ms). The overlap is counted twice and the result is an impossible −75 ms. The real self-time is 10 ms: the parent's 100 ms minus the 90 ms covered by *at least one* child (5–95). Tracing UIs compute the **union** of child intervals; when you compute self-time yourself, you must too (`distributed-tracing-m3`).

### Querying and pivoting

Section 1's dashboard tells you *that* something is wrong. To find out *why*, you compare **cohorts**: groups of requests that differ in outcome. The question is never "show me the errors"; it is **"what do failing requests have in common that successful ones don't?"**

**The pivot path**

1. **Metric:** error % for `POST /api/orders` jumps (dashboard).
2. **Exemplars:** many metrics backends attach example trace IDs to histogram buckets. Click the spike and open a few failing traces.
3. **Trace:** see which span has error status and which attributes it carries.
4. **Logs:** filter logs by that trace ID to read the full event detail.
5. **Cohort query:** group all requests by candidate attributes and compare error rates.

### Sampling: keeping the traces that matter

Tracing every request can be expensive. At 2 million Brewline requests a day, spans cost real money to send, store and index. **Sampling** keeps only some traces.

- **Head sampling:** decide at the *start* of the trace (e.g., keep 1%). It is cheap and simple, but at the start you don't know whether the request will fail or be slow.
- **Tail sampling:** buffer spans briefly, then decide at the *end* using the whole trace: keep all errors, keep all slow requests, keep a small % of the rest. It costs more (a collector must hold spans until the trace completes), but it keeps the interesting traces.

The sampling decision must travel with the context (the `01`/`00` flag in `traceparent`), so every hop keeps or drops the same trace. Otherwise you get fragments.

### ⚠️ Common errors

1. **Assuming tracing needs microservices.** A monolith plus browser plus DB already has boundaries worth tracing. *(`distributed-tracing-m1`)*
2. **Stopping at auto-instrumentation.** Unexplained self-time is where your business logic hides. *(`distributed-tracing-m2`)*
3. **Putting IDs in span names** (`charge order 8812`). This destroys grouping. Use attributes. *(`structured-logging-m2`, carried over from Section 1)*
4. **Blaming the span with the longest duration.** The root always "wins"; look at self-time. *(`distributed-tracing-m3`)*
5. **Subtracting child durations when children run in parallel.** You get negative self-time; use the union of intervals.
6. **Missing CORS or propagation-URL configuration for `traceparent`.** The trace splits silently. *(`request-correlation-m2`)*
7. **Believing a 200 response means the user saw the right thing.** *(`frontend-observability-m1`)*
8. **Relying on "someone will see it in the console".** *(`frontend-observability-m2`)*
9. **Searching for the error text instead of comparing cohorts.** *(`telemetry-querying-m1`)*
10. **Filtering with `<>` or `NOT IN` on columns that contain NULLs, then concluding "none".** *(`telemetry-querying-m2`)*
11. **Uniform head sampling at a low rate.** Most rare errors are thrown away before anyone looks. *(`instrumentation-tradeoffs-m1`)*

## Misconceptions to watch for in this section

- **"Tracing is only for microservices"** (`distributed-tracing-m1`). Boundaries, not service count, make tracing useful.
- **"Auto-instrumentation gives you everything"** (`distributed-tracing-m2`). Unexplained self-time is where your business logic hides.
- **"Span duration equals work done in that service"** (`distributed-tracing-m3`). Duration includes waiting; use self-time.
- **"If the API returned 200, the frontend is fine"** (`frontend-observability-m1`). Valid responses can still break UI state.
- **"Search for the error message and read the matches"** (`telemetry-querying-m1`). Compare cohorts instead.
- **"Sample 1% uniformly and you'll be fine"** (`instrumentation-tradeoffs-m1`). Uniform head sampling throws away most rare errors.

## Lab 2: One trace per click (practical activity, about 45 minutes)

**Goal:** a customer's **Place Order** click produces one connected trace from browser to database and payment provider; client state events link to that trace; and you can pivot from a dashboard spike to exemplar traces and logs.

1. **Backend auto-instrumentation (5 min).** Enable HTTP, framework and DB auto-instrumentation. Set the log `requestId` equal to the active trace ID so Lab 1's logs join the traces.
2. **Manual spans (10 min).** Add `pricing.calculate`, `inventory.reserve` and `payments.charge` with attributes `store.id`, `order.item_count` and `payment.provider`. No span name may contain an ID.
3. **Browser propagation (10 min).** Enable frontend tracing and fetch instrumentation, configure propagation to the API origin, and add `traceparent` to the API's CORS `Access-Control-Allow-Headers`. Use your fixed `tracedFetch`. Verify that one trace ID contains browser, API, DB and payments spans.
4. **Client telemetry (10 min).** Emit `cart.request_sent`, `cart.response_applied` (with `cart_items`), `cart.state_changed` and uncaught errors via `buildClientEvent`, shipped with `sendBeacon`.
5. **Sampling (5 min).** Configure a tail-sampling policy equivalent to `shouldKeepTrace`: all errors, root ≥ 1,000 ms (capped per route), 5% of the rest. Justify it in two sentences.
6. **Pivot drill (5 min).** Flip the load generator's `adyen-timeout` switch. Go from the error-% panel to an exemplar trace, to the failing span's attributes, to logs filtered by trace ID, to a cohort query grouped by `payment_provider`. Record each step.

**Acceptance checklist**

- One trace containing browser, API, DB and payments spans under a single trace ID.
- At least three manual spans, each with a business attribute and a low-variety name.
- One `cart.state_changed` event whose `traceId` opens the matching backend trace.
- A sampling policy with a two-sentence justification.
- Pivot-drill notes: metric → trace → logs → cohort query, with the query and its result.

## Section 2 summary: what you should now believe

1. A **trace** is one user action's timeline across every boundary; **spans** have low-variety names and carry variable data as **attributes**.
2. Auto-instrumentation gives you the skeleton; **manual spans** belong where business logic creates unexplained self-time.
3. **Propagation fails silently.** Verify one trace ID spans browser, API, DB and payments, including CORS and propagation-URL settings.
4. **Client telemetry** with `seq` and `traceId` is the only way to see UI failures that return 200.
5. Attribute latency by **self-time** using the union of child intervals, and find causes by **comparing cohorts**, not reading errors.
6. **Tail sampling** keeps every error and slow trace for roughly the cost of low-rate head sampling.

workedExamples.title: Choosing a sampling strategy
workedExamples.problem: Brewline serves **2,000,000 traces/day**. 0.2% are errors (4,000/day). 0.5% are slow, over 1 s (10,000/day). Choose a sampling strategy.
steps: **Uniform 1% head sampling** keeps ~20,000 traces/day: about **40 errors** and **100 slow** traces. During an incident affecting 0.2% of requests you would have a handful of examples, possibly none from the failing store.
**Tail sampling (keep errors + slow + 1% of the rest)** keeps 4,000 errors + 10,000 slow (at most 14,000, less if they overlap) + 1% of the remaining ~1,986,000 (≈19,860). Total ≈ **33,860/day**.
**Compare:** about 1.7× the volume of 1% head sampling, but **100×** as many error traces and **100×** as many slow traces.
**Bound the cost:** cap the keep-slow rule (e.g., at most 50 slow traces per route per minute) so a site-wide slowdown can't flood the backend.
workedExamples.conclusion: Choose tail sampling with keep-errors, keep-slow (capped) and a small baseline. Justify it by the questions you must answer during an incident, not by a percentage that sounds cheap.

sections.title: Make It Confess: Telemetry-Only Debugging Capstone
sections.description: Using only the telemetry built in Sections 1–2, diagnose three seeded bugs (an intermittent 500, a slow endpoint and a broken frontend state), prove root cause with evidence, and close the instrumentation gaps the investigation exposes.

Checkout fails for 25% of orders; `api-2` fails more than `api-1`. Before you start: is `api-2` the problem?

sectionSummary.content:
## Section 3 summary: what you should now believe

1. **Investigate with a loop**: observe, hypothesize, predict, run a discriminating query, record the verdict, and write it all down.
2. **Intermittent means a hidden variable.** Compare cohorts, including combinations of attributes, until one explains 100% of failures and 0% of successes.
3. **Check your data before your conclusions.** NULLs vanish from `AVG`, `MAX` and `COUNT(column)`, and the worst case is often the one that is missing.
4. **Patterns beat single spans.** Hundreds of identical fast spans (N+1) can cost more than one slow one.
5. **Healthy APIs can produce broken UIs.** Client events ordered by `seq` and linked by `traceId` expose races the server never sees.
6. **Every investigation ends with a gap fix**: small, bounded and safe, aimed at the question that was slow to answer.
keyTakeaways: Run the **loop** and keep an **evidence log**.
A root cause **explains every failure and no successes**.
Start frontend bugs from **client events** linked by `traceId`.
Finish with a **bounded, safe gap fix**.

contentBlocks.content:
## Why this matters

The bugs that hurt most in production are the ones you can't reproduce on your laptop. They depend on real data (one store's menu), real timing (two responses racing) or real scale (a customer with 600 orders). Reproducing them locally means guessing the conditions; when you can't, it means reading code and hoping.

This capstone takes the guessing away. You get three bugs, no debugger and no local repro. You may open source code **only after** your telemetry has named a specific place to look, and only to write the fix. The skill you practise is the one you'll need on your next incident: turning "something is wrong for some users" into "*this* is wrong, for *these* requests, *because of this*, and here is the evidence", in minutes instead of days.

## What you will be able to do

| # | Objective |
|---|---|
| 3.1 | Apply a hypothesis-driven loop (observe → hypothesize → query → confirm or refute) and record each step as an evidence log. |
| 3.2 | Diagnose the intermittent 500 by isolating the hidden variable that separates failing from succeeding requests via cohort queries. |
| 3.3 | Diagnose the slow endpoint by moving from dashboard latency percentiles to exemplar traces and pinpointing the responsible span and cause. |
| 3.4 | Diagnose the broken frontend state by correlating client-side state telemetry with the backend trace for the same user action. |
| 3.5 | Distinguish root cause from correlated symptoms by showing the chosen hypothesis explains all observations, including unaffected requests. |
| 3.6 | Identify at least one instrumentation gap that slowed the investigation, add the missing telemetry and justify its cost and safety trade-offs. |

**Each bug leans on a different signal family:** the intermittent 500 on logs and cohorts (Section 1), the slow endpoint on metrics and traces (Sections 1–2), and the broken frontend state on client telemetry and trace correlation (Section 2).

### The investigation loop

**Concrete starting point.** You're told: *"Checkout sometimes fails."* The tempting move is to open `orders.js` and start reading. Reading code shows what *could* happen; it can't tell you what *did* happen, to whom and under what conditions. Timing-, data- and load-dependent bugs can't be seen in code at all.

### Key terms

- **Observation:** a fact read from telemetry, with its source, such as "Error % for `POST /api/orders` is 25% over the incident window (query Q1)."
- **Hypothesis:** a testable explanation that predicts what *other* telemetry should show if it is true.
- **Discriminating query:** a query whose result would differ depending on whether the hypothesis is true or false.
- **Evidence log:** a running record of each observation, hypothesis, query and verdict.
- **Root cause:** the condition that, if removed, would stop the failures. It must explain **every** observation, including the requests that did *not* fail.
- **Symptom (correlated signal):** something that changes alongside the failure but doesn't cause it, such as higher CPU or more errors on one instance.

**The loop**

```text
 observe ──► hypothesize ──► predict ("if true, query X will show Y")
    ▲                                   │
    │                                   ▼
 record ◄──── confirm / refute ◄──── run query X
```

**Evidence log template** (use it for every bug in this section):

| # | Observation (with source) | Hypothesis | Prediction | Query / pivot | Result | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

**Capstone rules**

1. No debugger, no local reproduction, no reading code to *find* the bug.
2. Every claim cites a query, trace or dashboard panel.
3. You may open code once telemetry names a file or function, to confirm and fix it.
4. A root cause must pass the "explains all" test (lesson: *Root cause vs. symptom*).

### The practice incident dataset (Incident Pack A)

The worked investigations use a snapshot of Brewline telemetry during an incident, in four tables:

| Table | Contents | Built in |
|---|---|---|
| `requests` | One row per request at the gateway: `trace_id`, `route`, `status`, `duration_ms`, `store_id`, `item`, `user_id`, `instance` | Sections 1–2 |
| `logs` | Structured error events: `trace_id`, `level`, `event`, `error_message` | Section 1 |
| `spans` | Server spans: `trace_id`, `span_id`, `parent_id`, `name`, `start_ms`, `duration_ms` | Section 2 |
| `client_events` | Browser telemetry: `session_id`, `seq`, `ts_ms`, `trace_id`, `event`, `cart_items` | Section 2 |

A `status` or `duration_ms` of NULL means the client gave up before the gateway logged a response. The `/history` span rows are generated by a recursive query: one `db.query order_items` span per order the user has.

The scratch space below has the whole dataset loaded (locked) above an editable query. Explore it before the investigations: try `SELECT route, COUNT(*) FROM requests GROUP BY route;`.

The **capstone** at the end of this section uses a different set of seeded bugs (Incident Pack B) in your own instrumented Brewline, so these worked investigations teach the method without giving away the capstone answers.

interactionSequence.prompt: Hypothesis: "instance `api-2` is broken." Which query would **discriminate** between this hypothesis being true or false?
options: Error rate of POST /api/orders grouped by instance
SELECT * FROM logs WHERE level = 'error'
Average latency of all routes over the last day
Reading the deploy history for api-2

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct: if api-2 is broken, api-1 should be (near) clean; if both fail, the hypothesis is refuted.
Reading error lines shows symptoms, not whether the failures differ by instance.
Averages across routes can't test an instance hypothesis, and they hide tails.
Deploy history might suggest a cause but doesn't test whether failures are confined to api-2.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A discriminating query gives **different results** depending on whether the hypothesis is true. Grouping by the suspected variable and comparing groups is the most common form.

## Case: the intermittent 500

Follow the worked investigation step by step, then try the faded version on a new report, then write the decisive query yourself.

interactionSequence.prompt: In Incident Pack A, every failure is at `harbor` but only half of harbor's orders fail. What does that tell you about `store_id`?
options: It is necessary but not sufficient: look for a second variable that separates harbor's failures from its successes
Harbor is broken; roll back its configuration
The failures at harbor are random
Store is irrelevant because it isn't 100%

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct: combine it with another candidate (here, `item`).
Half of harbor's orders succeed, so 'harbor is broken' doesn't explain the successes.
Intermittent failures almost always hide another variable.
It is 100% of the failures; it just isn't the whole story.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: When a variable covers all failures but also many successes, it is a **necessary** condition. Look for the interaction that makes it sufficient.

Incident Pack A is loaded.

hints: You wrote this shape in Section 2's provider challenge; now group by two columns.
Row filters go in `WHERE`; filters on aggregates (at least one error) go in `HAVING`.
`HAVING SUM(CASE WHEN status >= 500 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) > 0`, and use `100.0` to avoid integer division.

SELECT store_id,
       item,
       COUNT(*) AS requests,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status >= 500 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS errors,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN status >= 500 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS error_pct
FROM requests
WHERE route = 'POST /api/orders'
GROUP BY store_id, item
HAVING SUM(CASE WHEN status >= 500 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) > 0
ORDER BY error_pct DESC, store_id, item;

workedExamples.problem: **Report:** "Checkout sometimes fails with a 500. Retrying sometimes works." Use Incident Pack A.
steps:
**Observe.** The dashboard shows `POST /api/orders` at a 25% error rate (4 of 16 requests in the window). The logs for the failures:

```sql
SELECT trace_id, error_message FROM logs WHERE event = 'order.failed';
```

| trace_id | error_message |
|---|---|
| o02 | TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'amount') |
| o05 | TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'amount') |
| o09 | TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'amount') |
| o13 | TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'amount') |

This tells you *what* crashed, not *which requests* or *why only some*.
**Hypothesize.** "Intermittent" usually means "depends on a variable we haven't looked at yet". Candidates from the event schema: `store_id`, `item`, `instance`, `user_id`.

**Run discriminating queries**: group by each candidate and compare error rates.

*By instance:*

| instance | requests | errors | error_pct |
|---|---|---|---|
| api-2 | 9 | 3 | 33.3 |
| api-1 | 7 | 1 | 14.3 |

*By store:*

| store_id | requests | errors | error_pct |
|---|---|---|---|
| harbor | 8 | 4 | 50.0 |
| airport | 4 | 0 | 0.0 |
| midtown | 4 | 0 | 0.0 |

*By item:*

| item | requests | errors | error_pct |
|---|---|---|---|
| pumpkin-latte | 7 | 4 | 57.1 |
| cold-brew | 5 | 0 | 0.0 |
| flat-white | 4 | 0 | 0.0 |

**Read carefully.** Instance looks suspicious (`api-2` 33% vs `api-1` 14%), but `api-1` fails too, so an instance problem can't be the whole story: the *first anomaly* trap. Every failure is at `harbor`, but half of harbor's orders succeed. Every failure is a `pumpkin-latte`, but 3 of 7 succeed. Store and item are each **necessary but not sufficient**.

**Combine the two necessary conditions:**

| store_id | item | requests | errors | error_pct |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| harbor | pumpkin-latte | 4 | 4 | 100.0 |

**Apply the 'explains all' test.** Hypothesis: *orders for `pumpkin-latte` at `harbor` fail.* It explains all 4 failures; it matches **zero** successes (pumpkin lattes elsewhere succeed, other harbor items succeed); it explains the `TypeError` on `amount` (a price lookup returning null for one store–item pair); and it explains the instance skew as routing coincidence (3 of the 4 harbor pumpkin orders happened to land on `api-2`).
**Now open code.** Telemetry points at the price lookup for (store, item). `menu_prices` has `harbor/pumpkin-latte` with `price = NULL`: the seasonal item launched without a harbor price.
workedExamples.conclusion: 25% order errors → all share `TypeError … 'amount'` → cohort grouping isolates **harbor × pumpkin-latte** (100% vs 0% elsewhere) → the hypothesis explains every failure and no successes → the missing price row confirms it. **Gap noticed:** `order.failed` lacked `storeId` and `item`, so the investigation needed a join.

workedExamples.problem: **Report:** the Section 1 dashboard shows `GET /api/orders/history` p99 = 2,020 ms (baseline 190) with p50 unchanged. You saw in the prediction exercise that one request has no recorded status or duration.
steps: **Observe, and check the data.** `COUNT(*) = 8` but `COUNT(status) = 7`: request `h06` was abandoned by the client before the gateway logged a response, so it is invisible to `AVG` and `MAX`.
**Hypothesize.** p50 is normal and the tail is huge, so something about *specific requests* makes them slow. Candidates: particular users, particular instances, a slow dependency.

**Pivot to server spans**, which exist even for `h06` because the server finished its work after the client left:

```sql
SELECT r.trace_id,
       r.user_id,
       root.duration_ms AS server_ms,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM spans c
         WHERE c.trace_id = r.trace_id AND c.name LIKE 'db.%') AS db_calls
FROM requests r
JOIN spans root ON root.trace_id = r.trace_id AND root.parent_id IS NULL
WHERE r.route = 'GET /api/orders/history'
ORDER BY server_ms DESC, r.trace_id;
```

| trace_id | user_id | server_ms | db_calls |
|---|---|---|---|
| h06 | u-90 | 4820 | 601 |
| h03 | u-31 | 2020 | 251 |
| h08 | u-63 | 1940 | 241 |
| h05 | u-48 | 164 | 19 |
| h02 | u-22 | 116 | 13 |
| h07 | u-22 | 116 | 13 |
| h01 | u-17 | 44 | 4 |
| h04 | u-17 | 44 | 4 |

**Read it.** Server time grows in lockstep with the number of DB calls: 4 calls → 44 ms; 251 → 2,020 ms; 601 → 4,820 ms. Both instances appear among fast and slow rows. Slowness is about **how many DB calls the request makes**.

**Which span?** Sum child time across the slow traces:

```sql
SELECT c.name,
       COUNT(*)           AS spans,
       SUM(c.duration_ms) AS total_ms
FROM spans c
JOIN spans root ON root.trace_id = c.trace_id AND root.parent_id IS NULL
WHERE c.parent_id IS NOT NULL
  AND root.duration_ms >= 1000
GROUP BY c.name
ORDER BY total_ms DESC;
```

| name | spans | total_ms |
|---|---|---|
| db.query order_items | 1090 | 8720 |
| db.query orders | 3 | 36 |
| cache.get user_prefs | 3 | 9 |

`db.query order_items` accounts for 8,720 of 8,765 ms. Each call is fast (8 ms); there are just hundreds of them. A slow trace's waterfall shows a staircase of identical spans: the **N+1 query** pattern.

**Explains all?** Users with few orders are fast, users with hundreds are slow, and the aborted request belongs to the user with 600 orders. The unchanged p50 fits (most users have few orders). `cache.get` and `db.query orders` are constant and tiny, so they are not causes.
workedExamples.conclusion: The `/history` tail is caused by an **N+1 pattern** loading order items: cost grows by ~8 ms per order, and the worst case (600 orders) exceeds the client timeout. Fix: load items for all orders in one query. **Gaps noticed:** the gateway recorded no duration for aborted requests, and the root span lacked an `orders.count` attribute.

workedExamples.title: Investigation 3: the broken frontend state
workedExamples.problem: **Report:** "I removed oat milk, the cart showed one item, then when I checked out it showed two items again."
steps:
**Observe the backend first:**

```sql
SELECT trace_id, status, duration_ms FROM requests
WHERE route = 'PUT /api/cart' AND trace_id IN ('c3','c4') ORDER BY trace_id;
```

| trace_id | status | duration_ms |
|---|---|---|
| c3 | 200 | 640 |
| c4 | 200 | 90 |

Both returned 200. If you stopped here you would close the ticket as "can't reproduce".
**Hypothesize.** The server's final cart is correct, so the wrong state was created in the browser: either the UI mishandled a response, or responses were applied in the wrong order.

**Reconstruct the session timeline** from client events ordered by `seq` (the runnable example below prints this):

```text
+   0ms #1 c3 cart.request_sent
+ 150ms #2 c4 cart.request_sent
+ 241ms #3 c4 cart.response_applied items=1
+ 641ms #4 c3 cart.response_applied items=2
```

**Read it.** c3 (add muffin) was sent first; c4 (remove oat milk) 150 ms later. c4's response came back fast and was applied (1 item). Then c3's slow response arrived and overwrote the cart with an older snapshot (2 items). Whatever arrives last wins.

**Find every session with the same pattern:**

```sql
SELECT late.session_id,
       late.trace_id   AS stale_trace,
       early.trace_id  AS overwritten_trace,
       late.cart_items AS items_shown
FROM client_events late
JOIN client_events late_sent
  ON late_sent.trace_id = late.trace_id AND late_sent.event = 'cart.request_sent'
JOIN client_events early
  ON early.session_id = late.session_id
 AND early.event = 'cart.response_applied'
 AND early.seq < late.seq
JOIN client_events early_sent
  ON early_sent.trace_id = early.trace_id AND early_sent.event = 'cart.request_sent'
WHERE late.event = 'cart.response_applied'
  AND late_sent.seq < early_sent.seq;
```

| session_id | stale_trace | overwritten_trace | items_shown |
|---|---|---|---|
| s-31 | c3 | c4 | 2 |

Session `s-12` made requests too but isn't returned: its responses arrived in order.

**Explains all?** The hypothesis predicts the bug only when an earlier request is slower than a later one: `s-31` had 640 ms then 90 ms; `s-12`'s requests were similar in speed. It explains the 200s, the correct server state and the wrong UI.
workedExamples.conclusion: A **client-side race** in how cart responses are applied. Fix: tag each request with a sequence number and ignore any response older than the last one applied. **Gap noticed:** there was no event for "response dropped as stale"; add a `cart.stale_response_dropped` counter to confirm the fix and measure how often the race happens.

contentBlocks.content:
### Root cause vs. symptom, and closing the gaps

**The "explains all" test (Objective 3.5).** A hypothesis is a root cause only if it:
1. explains **every failing** request
2. matches **no (or almost no) succeeding** requests
3. explains the **other observations** (error text, timing, the odd instance skew)
4. predicts something you then **confirmed** with a new query

In Investigation 1:

| Hypothesis | Failures matched | Successes matched | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| `api-2` is broken | 3 of 4 | 6 | Symptom |
| `harbor` store is broken | 4 of 4 | 4 | Necessary but not sufficient |
| `harbor` × `pumpkin-latte` | 4 of 4 | 0 | Root cause |

The challenge in this lesson turns the test into a function.

**Closing instrumentation gaps (Objective 3.6).** Every investigation ends with the question: *what telemetry would have made this faster?* Then you add it, and check its cost and safety as in Section 1.

### ⚠️ Common errors

1. **Opening the code first.** You find three plausible bugs, none of which is the real one. *(`production-diagnosis-m1`)*
2. **Stopping at the first skewed group** (`api-2` fails more). Always check whether the skew explains *all* failures and *no* successes. *(`production-diagnosis-m2`)*
3. **Calling it "random" or "flaky" and adding retries.** Intermittent failures almost always have a hidden variable. *(`production-diagnosis-m3`)*
4. **Reading error messages one by one** instead of comparing failing and succeeding cohorts. *(`telemetry-querying-m1`)*
5. **Trusting `AVG`/`COUNT(column)` over data with NULLs.** Aborted and timed-out requests vanish from the numbers. *(`telemetry-querying-m2`, `metrics-instrumentation-m1`)*
6. **Closing frontend tickets because the API returned 200.** *(`frontend-observability-m1`)*
7. **Blaming the span with the largest single duration** rather than the pattern (hundreds of small identical spans). *(`distributed-tracing-m3`)*
8. **Fixing the gap with "log everything".** Add the specific fields, bounded metrics and events that answer the slow question. *(`structured-logging-m1`, `instrumentation-tradeoffs-m2`)*

## Misconceptions to watch for in this section

- **"I'll find it faster by reading the code"** (`production-diagnosis-m1`). Code shows what *could* happen; telemetry shows what *did*.
- **"The first anomaly I see is the cause"** (`production-diagnosis-m2`). `api-2` erroring more was a coincidence of routing.
- **"Intermittent means random"** (`production-diagnosis-m3`). 50% at harbor and 57% for pumpkin latte became 100% and 0% in combination.
- **"If the query returned nothing, the event didn't happen"** (`telemetry-querying-m2`). The aborted request vanished from `AVG` and `MAX`.
- **"If the API returned 200, the frontend is fine"** (`frontend-observability-m1`). Every cart request succeeded; the UI was still wrong.

workedExamples.title: Closing the Investigation 1 gap
workedExamples.problem: Investigation 1 needed a join to learn which store and item each failed order involved. Close the gap.
steps: **Gap:** `order.failed` lacked `storeId` and `item`, so you needed a join, and in a real log tool that join may not be possible.
**Add:** fields `storeId`, `item` and `priceSource` on `order.failed`, and a new `warn` event `menu.price_missing` with `storeId` and `item`, emitted at the lookup when a price is NULL.

**Metric:** a counter `menu_price_missing_total{store_id}`. `store_id` has 3 values, so it is bounded. **Not** `item`: the menu changes seasonally and the item set grows, so item goes in the log event.
**Safety:** no customer data is added, only menu identifiers.
**Cost:** one extra event only on a rare failure path; three new series.
**Payoff:** the dashboard can show 'price missing at harbor' directly, and an alert on `menu_price_missing_total > 0` would have caught this before customers did.
workedExamples.conclusion: A gap fix is a **small, bounded, safe** change aimed at the exact question that was slow to answer. It is not "log everything next time".

fadedVariant.problem: Close the gaps from **Investigation 2** (the slow `/history` endpoint): aborted requests had no duration, and the correlation with order count took three queries to see.
givenSteps: **Gaps:** (a) the gateway logged no `durationMs` or `outcome` when the client aborted; (b) the root span had no attribute for how many orders were loaded.

blankedStepAnswers: Record `durationMs` (time until abort) and `outcome: "client_aborted"` on the gateway's completion event. It adds no personal data and stops the worst cases vanishing from latency statistics.
An `orders.count` **span attribute** on the root span (and the `history.loaded` log event). Not a metric label: order counts are unbounded.
Two extra fields on events that already exist and one span attribute; no new time series.

## Capstone: debug Incident Pack B using only your telemetry (practical activity, about 80 minutes)

**Setup.** Deploy your instrumented Brewline from Labs 1–2 with the **Incident Pack B** flag enabled and start the load generator. Three bugs are now live. You have the log store, metrics dashboard, tracing UI, client telemetry and SQL access to the exported telemetry tables.

**Rules**

1. No debugger, no local reproduction, no reading code until telemetry has named a specific function or file.
2. Every claim in your write-up cites a query, trace ID or dashboard panel.

**The three reports**

| Bug | Report | Time box |
|---|---|---|
| B1: intermittent 500 | "Some customers get 'Something went wrong' at checkout. It doesn't happen to me." | 25 min |
| B2: slow endpoint | "Placing an order is sometimes really slow, like 5+ seconds." | 25 min |
| B3: broken frontend state | "The confirmation page says my order will be ready in 'NaN minutes'." | 20 min |
| Gap fix and write-up | | 10 min |

**For each bug, deliver:** an evidence log with at least 4 rows; the discriminating query or trace pivot with its result; a root-cause statement that passes the "explains all" test; and one instrumentation gap you hit, the telemetry you added and a two-line cost and safety justification.

**Rubric (per bug, 10 points)**

| Criterion | Points |
|---|---|
| Evidence log shows a real loop (hypotheses refuted as well as confirmed) | 3 |
| Discriminating query or pivot is correct and its result is cited | 3 |
| Root cause passes "explains all" (failing and unaffected requests addressed) | 2 |
| Gap fix is specific, bounded and safe, with justification | 2 |

Submit your conclusion for each bug in the scenario questions below **after** you finish its evidence log. The feedback then shows the seeded cause so you can check your chain of evidence.

## Section 3 summary: what you should now believe

1. **Investigate with a loop**: observe, hypothesize, predict, run a discriminating query, record the verdict, and write it all down.
2. **Intermittent means a hidden variable.** Compare cohorts, including combinations of attributes, until one explains 100% of failures and 0% of successes.
3. **Check your data before your conclusions.** NULLs vanish from `AVG`, `MAX` and `COUNT(column)`, and the worst case is often the one that is missing.
4. **Patterns beat single spans.** Hundreds of identical fast spans (N+1) can cost more than one slow one.
5. **Healthy APIs can produce broken UIs.** Client events ordered by `seq` and linked by `traceId` expose races the server never sees.
6. **Every investigation ends with a gap fix**: small, bounded and safe, aimed at the question that was slow to answer.

This exercise happens outside the course. It is formative and never blocks progress.

glossary.definition: One record describing one thing that happened, stored as named fields rather than a sentence.
The agreed list of field names, types and meanings shared by every event in a service.
How urgent an event is (`debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error`); drives retention, sampling and alerting.
Emitting log events that follow a schema so machines can filter, group and count them.
A unique value generated once per incoming request and attached to every event that request produces; also called a correlation ID.
Carrying request or trace context from one piece of code or service to the next, across `await`, queues and HTTP calls.
Per-request data (request ID, user, route) available anywhere in that request's async chain, e.g. via AsyncLocalStorage.
A metric that only goes up, such as total requests; charted as a per-second rate.
A metric that goes up and down, such as open DB connections.
Counts of observations in value ranges (buckets), from which percentiles are computed.
The value that a given share of observations are at or below; p99 = 250 ms means 99% took 250 ms or less.
A key–value pair that splits a metric into separate time series, such as `route="POST /api/orders"`.
The number of distinct time series a metric produces: the product of each label's distinct values.
Track Rate, Errors and Duration for every request-serving service.
The full record of one operation as it moves through every component, identified by a trace ID.
One timed unit of work inside a trace, with a name, duration, parent, status and attributes.
Key–value details on a span, such as `store.id=harbor`; the tracing equivalent of log fields.
The span with no parent, where a trace began.
A timeline view of a trace, with each span drawn as a bar under its parent.
The W3C header that carries the trace ID, parent span ID and sampled flag between services.
Libraries that create spans automatically for HTTP requests, outbound calls and queries.
The part of a span's duration not covered by any child span.
Grouping requests by candidate attributes and comparing outcomes between groups to find what failing requests share.
An example trace ID attached to a metric data point, used to jump from a chart to a trace.
Deciding whether to keep a trace at its start, before the outcome is known.
Deciding whether to keep a trace after it completes, so errors and slow traces can always be kept.
A per-session counter on client events that records true event order regardless of clock accuracy.
A running record of observations, hypotheses, predictions, queries, results and verdicts during an investigation.
A query whose result differs depending on whether a hypothesis is true.
The condition that, if removed, stops the failures; it must explain every failure and no successes.
A signal that changes alongside a failure but does not cause it.
Loading a list with one query and then running one more query per item, so cost grows with data size.
Missing telemetry that slowed or blocked an investigation.
Replacing sensitive values (emails, card numbers, tokens) in telemetry before it is shipped.
